analysis.one_liner: Lets states open Medicaid to any resident as a low-cost public health insurance option.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with 17 Democratic cosponsors in March 2024, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any state offer its residents the choice to buy into Medicaid — the government health program that generally costs less than private insurance — as long as they aren't eligible for Medicaid already and don't have other coverage. States could charge premiums capped at 8.5% of household income, and regular ACA subsidies could help pay them. The bill also offers a permanent enhanced federal matching rate to the ten states that never expanded Medicaid, requires Medicaid in every state to cover comprehensive reproductive health care including abortion, and raises Medicaid payments for primary care to Medicare levels.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states that choose to offer the buy-in — especially people who earn too much for Medicaid but can't afford marketplace plans, or find marketplace coverage inadequate. People in the ten holdout states would gain if the permanent enhanced federal match finally lures their states into expansion. Medicaid enrollees nationwide would gain a guaranteed right to comprehensive reproductive care, including abortion. Primary care doctors, nurse practitioners, and community clinics would be paid Medicare-level rates for their Medicaid patients.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured residents in participating states

how_it_helps.text: Lets any state allow residents who lack other coverage to buy into Medicaid, with premiums capped at 8.5% of household income and ACA-style limits on cost-sharing [S2][S3].
Lets enrollees use ACA premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions to help pay for the Medicaid buy-in coverage [S3].
Gives the ten states that never expanded Medicaid a permanent enhanced federal matching rate (starting at 90%) whenever they expand, instead of the phased rate that expired [S2][S3].
Requires every state's Medicaid program to cover comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care, including abortion services, as a condition of plan approval [S2][S3].

Restores and expands the Medicaid primary care payment floor, paying family doctors, OB/GYNs, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, midwives, and community clinics at least Medicare rates for primary care [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear new costs: a 90% federal match for administering the buy-in program, a $50 million appropriation for quality measures, higher primary care payment rates, and the enhanced match for late-expanding states. Enrollees pay premiums and cost-sharing, though subsidies offset much of it. Private health insurers would lose customers in states that offer the cheaper public option.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and private health insurers

drawbacks.text: The program is entirely optional for states, so residents in states that decline to offer it — including most of the states with the worst uninsured rates — would get nothing [S2][S3].
Buy-in enrollees can still be charged premiums up to 8.5% of income plus deductibles and copays, which for families near that cap approaches the cost of a marketplace plan [S3].
Mandating abortion coverage as a condition of Medicaid approval is a hard line that guaranteed opposition and almost certainly narrowed the bill's support to one party [S2][S3].
Raising Medicaid primary care rates to Medicare levels adds federal and state costs, and the bill does not say how states' shares would be funded [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents of participating states, a Medicaid-based public option would likely be the cheapest comprehensive coverage available, with genuine protections against unaffordable premiums. But the state-by-state opt-in and the premium cap at 8.5% of income mean the benefit is uneven and, for some families, still expensive. The reproductive-care mandate is a significant coverage guarantee but carried real political cost. On balance a meaningful expansion of affordable coverage, paid for largely by federal taxpayers and by private insurers losing market share.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2024 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; the Congress ended in January 2025 with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the State Public Option Act on March 22, 2024, with 17 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the complete action history: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers keep the individual market uncontested by a cheaper public option, and states that have not expanded Medicaid keep the status quo. Residents without affordable coverage gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 supporters, including the sponsor and every cosponsor, were Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it never reached a vote.

industries.note: A Medicaid buy-in would be a cheaper public alternative to marketplace plans, taking customers and premium revenue from private insurers in participating states. The bill's death leaves the individual market uncontested.

industries.industry: Primary care providers (family doctors, OB/GYNs, nurse practitioners, community health centers)
industries.note: The bill requires Medicaid to pay at least Medicare rates for primary care, a raise for providers who treat Medicaid patients and an incentive for more doctors to accept them.
Buy-in enrollees could be served through managed care contracts, adding members, but the bill also requires those contracts to pass Medicare-level primary care rates through to providers.
Requiring Medicaid to cover abortion and related services would expand the pool of patients whose care is reimbursed with federal and state funds.
